items.question: Why is this absorption not merely an incidental mental state for us?
premises: An opponent may claim this absorption arises only by incidental context.
The world is not confined to mental exclusion or construction.
Beings have different tastes and inclinations.
items.inference: Therefore this absorption cannot be reduced to a merely incidental mental state.
uncertainties: The exact force of mānasāvarjī is slightly compressed in the compound.
items.plain_english: If someone objects that this absorption arises only incidentally, we do not accept that, because the world is not merely a mental construct and people have different inclinations.

rows.grounds: elements treated as divided from God

items.question: How does this nondual teaching differ from dualistic scriptures regarding the elements?
premises: In dualistic scriptures the elements are treated as separated from the supreme Lord.
This teaching is free from duality.
What is divided in dualism is not divided in the same way here.
items.inference: Therefore in this nondual system the elements are not regarded as separate from the supreme Lord.
uncertainties: bhūtādīnāṃ may include more than the gross elements, but the verse leaves the scope open.
items.plain_english: It is said that in dualistic scriptures the elements and so on are treated as separated from the supreme Lord, but in this teaching, which is free from duality, they are not regarded in that way.

rows.grounds: the full set of thirty-six principles

items.question: What is the true extent of Rudra's unobstructed power in this teaching?
premises: The thirty-six principles constitute the whole manifest system.
Anything else whatsoever is not outside that reality.
All of this is the great Goddess, Rudra's unobstructed power.
items.inference: Therefore nothing lies beyond the unobstructed power of Rudra.
items.plain_english: All that is comprised in the thirty-six principles, and anything else whatsoever, is nothing but the great Goddess, the unobstructed power of Rudra.

rows.grounds: reference to an earlier part of the work
the all-form nature of the lower principles
according to classifications like the fifteenfold

items.question: Why was the universal nature of earth and the other principles expounded earlier?
premises: Everything is the unobstructed power of Rudra.
The second section already expounded the universal form of earth and the other principles.
That exposition used divisions such as the fifteenfold.
items.inference: Therefore the earlier exposition of the elements as universal is consistent with their identity as Rudra's power.
uncertainties: The exact referent of pāñcadaśyādi is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: For that very reason, in the second section it was explained that earth and the other principles have a universal form, according to divisions such as the fifteenfold.

items.question: How should one understand the partless reality through differentiated aspects?
premises: In the earlier discussion, awareness of the partless arose through parts and subparts such as the qualities.
The same method applies in the present context.
Differentiated aspects can disclose an undivided reality.
items.inference: Therefore one should understand the partless reality here too through its differentiated aspects.
items.plain_english: Therefore, just as in the earlier discussion awareness of the partless reality arose through parts and subparts beginning with the qualities, so too it should be understood here.

rows.grounds: attributes grounded in its nature as power

items.question: By what kinds of attributes can the supreme reality be approached?
premises: The supreme reality can be approached through its attributes.
These include nonconceptuality, firmness, and sovereignty.
Because it is of the nature of power, its attributes inhere in itself.
items.inference: Therefore the supreme reality may be approached through its own intrinsic attributes as power.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically compressed and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: Therefore, through its own intrinsic attributes as power—such as nonconceptuality, firmness, sovereignty, or others—the supreme reality can be approached.

items.question: How do people shaped by conceptual impressions worship the supreme Lord?
premises: Some worshippers approach the Lord wholly and others partially.
Their approach is shaped by streams of conceptual impressions.
These impressions arise from what they have heard in scripture.
items.inference: Therefore even conceptually conditioned worshippers can approach the all-pervading supreme Lord.
uncertainties: The compound vikalpaughasaṃskārādye is compact; the agent sense is inferred from context.
items.plain_english: Those whose minds are shaped by streams of conceptual impressions arising from scripture worship that all-pervading supreme Lord, either wholly or partially.

rows.grounds: the Lord as substrate of attributes
they attain identity with the fully qualified Lord

items.question: How do conceptually mediated worshippers come to rest in the Lord himself?
premises: The worshippers engage attributes that shine within their own concepts.
Through skillful engagement with those attributes they approach their possessor.
They come to rest in the Lord as non-different from the full mass of his attributes.
items.inference: Therefore conceptual worship can culminate in non-difference from the fully qualified Lord.
items.plain_english: Because the attributes shining within their own concepts become vivid and skillfully grasped, they come to rest in the Lord himself, the possessor of attributes, as non-different from the full mass of his powers.

items.question: Why does the Lord's nonconceptual nature not prevent clear conceptual experience?
premises: The Lord's nature is nonconceptual and not born of the senses.
Conceptualization does not make that nature its object.
Yet clear experiences with inwardly drawn forms do arise.
items.inference: Therefore the Lord's nonconceptual nature can still be the ground of clear conceptual experiences.
uncertainties: The citation is attributed generally to the lord of sacred knowledge; the exact source text is not named here.
items.plain_english: For this reason the revered lord of sacred knowledge said: if conceptual thought cannot make your nonconceptual nature its object, then clear experiences with forms drawn within awareness would not arise.

items.question: Where is the Lord described as manifesting through the rays of his own power?
premises: The revered Matanga and related scriptures discuss the Lord's manifestation.
They describe it as consisting of rays of his own power.
They also speak of the Lord's abode with qualifying attributes.
items.inference: Therefore scriptural authority supports understanding the Lord's manifestation as his own power.
uncertainties: The verse only alludes to the cited passage rather than quoting it fully.
items.plain_english: This is stated in the revered Matanga and other texts, where the Lord's abode is described, with various qualifications, as consisting of the rays of his own power.

items.question: How is the supreme luminous reality characterized in that highest domain?
premises: The description concerns a supreme luminous domain.
That reality is brilliant, motionless, and unmoving in form.
It is the ultimate, supreme, subtle limit whose essence is nectar in all directions.
items.inference: Therefore the highest reality is a radiant, steady, and all-pervading supreme limit.
uncertainties: divi can suggest sky or light; the luminous sense fits the context best.
items.plain_english: In that luminous domain is the brilliantly radiant, motionless reality with unmoving form; that very reality is the supreme, subtle, ultimate limit, whose essence is nectar in all directions.

items.question: Why is the supreme reality spoken of as having a form?
premises: The supreme reality is without veils, peaceful, and beyond beginning and end.
It delights only in pure reality itself.
Even so, it is spoken of figuratively as having a form.
items.inference: Therefore the attribution of form to the supreme reality is a figurative usage, not a literal description.
items.plain_english: That excellent reality, with its veils destroyed, peaceful, delighting only in pure being, and beyond beginning and end, is nevertheless spoken of figuratively as having a form.

rows.grounds: explains the purpose of figurative form
by means of that figurative form
state of becoming one with it

items.question: What purpose does figuratively attributing form to the supreme serve?
premises: The supreme reality is spoken of figuratively as having form.
This figurative usage has a purpose.
Through it clarity arises and one quickly abides in identity with that reality.
items.inference: Therefore figurative form serves to make the supreme reality vivid and to support identity with it.
items.plain_english: This figurative way of speaking has a purpose: through it the reality becomes clear, and one quickly comes to abide in identity with that possessor of attributes.

rows.grounds: attributes presented as powers in suitable forms

items.question: Why are the Lord's attributes worshipped in various fitting forms?
premises: The attributes of the reality are called powers.
They are approached through various fitting forms.
Such worship aims at attaining identity with that reality.
items.inference: Therefore worship of the attributes as powers in fitting forms is a means to identity with the Lord.
items.plain_english: Those very attributes, called powers, are worshipped through various fitting forms so that one may attain identity with that reality.

rows.grounds: powers attract others depending on proximity

items.question: How can different powers draw in other powers during worship?
premises: Some powers are unlimited while others are limited.
Powers can draw in other powers.
This occurs according to the principle of nearness and distance.
items.inference: Therefore the scope of a contemplated power depends on whether it is limited or unlimited and on its relative nearness.
uncertainties: The compound at the end is dense; the intended logical principle is inferred from the surrounding doctrine.
items.plain_english: In that context, some power may be unlimited, or there may be limited powers; each can draw in others according to the principle of nearness and distance.

items.question: Why do the supreme attributes draw in all powers?
premises: Fullness, luminosity, consciousness, and Bhairava-identity are supreme attributes.
These attributes are all-pervasive.
What is all-pervasive can draw in all powers.
items.inference: Therefore contemplation of these supreme attributes draws in all the powers of the universe.
items.plain_english: Thus fullness of nature, luminosity, consciousness, and Bhairava-identity, because of their all-pervasiveness, draw in all the powers of the universe.

rows.grounds: lower deities lack full upward reach
the powers they can draw in
their reach depends on proximity in worship

items.question: Why do Sadashiva and other lower principles draw in powers only partially?
premises: Sadashiva and other principles do not pervade upward in the same way.
They are oriented toward lower levels.
Their worship draws in powers according to nearness or distance.
items.inference: Therefore Sadashiva and similar principles attract powers only in a limited, relative way.
uncertainties: adhojuṣaḥ is interpretive in nuance; it indicates orientation toward lower domains.
items.plain_english: But Sadashiva and the others, lacking full upward pervasion and oriented to lower levels, would draw in powers only according to how near or far their worship stands.

rows.grounds: refers to the mode just described

items.question: Why is the Shakta path described as conceptual in this context?
premises: The path just described is called the Shakta path.
It proceeds through a conceptual sequence.
Its conceptuality involves counterparts and distinctions.
items.inference: Therefore the Shakta path, as presented here, operates through conceptual distinctions.
uncertainties: pratiyogyavikalpakam is terse; it points to conceptuality structured by relational opposites.
items.plain_english: In this state, the path called Shakta has been described here as a conceptual course, because it proceeds through concepts involving counterparts and distinctions.

rows.grounds: any level from lowest to high

items.question: What happens when one established in the nonconceptual path enters through any level of reality?
premises: One may be established on the nonconceptual path.
Such a one may enter through any path from earth up to Sadashiva.
Any such entry can culminate in Shiva-identity.
items.inference: Therefore for one on the nonconceptual path, every level of reality can become a doorway to becoming Shiva.
items.plain_english: One who is established on the nonconceptual path, by whatever route he enters—from earth up to Sadashiva—by that very route he becomes Shiva.

rows.grounds: the heart illumined by the initial manifestation of reality
identity of consciousness with supreme Shiva

items.question: How does awareness reveal its identity as supreme Shiva in the purified heart?
premises: The heart becomes pure and luminous.
In that light the first manifest aspect of reality shines.
Through that very opening awareness stands as supreme Shiva.
items.inference: Therefore in the purified luminous heart, awareness reveals itself as supreme Shiva through its own manifestation.
uncertainties: bhūmyaṃśa is compact; it likely refers to an aspect or level of manifestation.
items.plain_english: In the pure heart, in the light where the first manifest aspect of reality shines, awareness itself stands forth, through that very opening, as supreme Shiva.

rows.grounds: the method grounded in supreme will

items.question: What do the wise call this immersion grounded in supreme will?
premises: The preceding method is grounded in a portion of supreme will-power.
It functions as a true means of realization.
Those of good understanding recognize it as a distinct immersion.
items.inference: Therefore the wise know this method as the Shambhava immersion.
uncertainties: sumatyantenivāsinaḥ is an unusual compound; the sense 'those dwelling in good understanding' is inferred.
items.plain_english: Thus those of good understanding know this true means, grounded in a portion of the supreme power of will, as the immersion called Shambhava.

rows.grounds: the powers appear in a maya-bound form

items.question: How is the Shakta mode described in relation to the inner faculties and maya?
premises: The Shakta mode involves mind, intellect, thought, and ego-making.
These operate clearly with conceptuality.
What appears as will and so on is maya-made in form, though not ultimately so in reality.
items.inference: Therefore the Shakta mode works through conceptual inner faculties while reinterpreting their maya-bound appearance.
uncertainties: The compound cetodhī-manohaṃkṛti compresses several inner functions; the gloss follows the standard grouping.
items.plain_english: Now the Shakta mode is described: mind, intellect, thought, and ego-making operate clearly with conceptuality, and what appears as will and so on is maya-made in form, though in reality otherwise.

items.question: How can the Shakta means, though based on maya, culminate in the nonconceptual?
premises: The Shakta mode proceeds through identification, intention, and determination.
It operates as a means within maya.
At its culmination it becomes nonconceptual.
items.inference: Therefore the Shakta means, though conceptually mediated, can lead beyond conceptuality.
items.plain_english: The Shakta mode proceeds through identification in the sequence of intention and determination; though it is a means operating within maya, at its culmination it becomes nonconceptual.

rows.grounds: states the condition of the bound being
obscured by limited subjectivity, revealed when it ceases

items.question: Why is the bound soul's nonconceptual state incomplete until the limited knower falls away?
premises: The bound soul can have a nonconceptual state.
That state is of the Shambhava kind but remains incomplete.
Its incompleteness is due to the defect of the limited knower, and it blossoms when that defect falls away.
items.inference: Therefore the bound soul's nonconceptual state becomes fully Shambhava only when limited subjectivity ceases.
uncertainties: mātṛdaurātmya is doctrinally loaded; rendered here as the defect or impairment of the limited knower.
items.plain_english: For the bound soul, the nonconceptual state is indeed of the Shambhava kind, but it remains incomplete because of the defect of the limited knower; when that falls away, it blossoms fully.
